title: Density
objective: After this level you can explain why some things float and others sink.
summary: Density is mass divided by volume. Things float when less dense than the liquid around them, so a log floats and a nail sinks. Ice is about 90 percent as dense as water, so it floats.

cards.headline: Solid water floats on liquid water. That's stranger than it sounds.
cards.body: Most substances pack tighter as they freeze, but water spreads out. That's why your ice cubes bob at the top of your drink. The explanation comes down to one idea: density.

cards.fact: Density is how much mass is packed into each bit of space.
cards.context: Divide an object's mass by its volume and you get its density. A kilogram of feathers and a kilogram of lead have exactly the same mass; the lead just crams it into far less space. Liquid water comes in at about 1 gram per cubic centimeter. Keep that number handy: it's the one everything gets compared to.

cards.headline: Float or sink? Compare densities
cards.body: Whether something floats doesn't depend on how heavy it is. It depends on density. If an object's average density is less than the liquid's, it floats; if it's denser, it sinks. That's why a huge log floats while a tiny iron nail sinks. The log is far heavier, but wood is less dense than water, and iron is denser.

mascot.line: People mix up heavy and dense. Heavy isn't the question; packed is.

cards.headline: Why ice floats
cards.body: When water freezes, its molecules lock into an open, roomy pattern that spreads them farther apart than in the liquid. Same mass, more space, so lower density: ice is only about 90 percent as dense as liquid water. Less dense means it floats. But only a little less dense, so it floats low, with most of an ice cube or an iceberg riding below the surface.
cards.callout: Ice: about 0.92 g per cm³. Liquid water: about 1.0.
